title: HIGH ENERGY-BOOSTING FOODS THAT CAN HELP FUEL YOUR NEXT WORKOUT
summary: You’ve probably heard the saying ‘food is fuel’, but what does that really mean, and how does it work?

blocks.text: You’ve probably heard the saying ‘food is fuel’, but what does that really mean, and how does it work?

Simply by being alive, our bodies are using energy. Pumping blood around the body, growing new cells, breathing, thinking, all use energy. And then on top of that, we need energy to move, talk, exercise, digest food, and more.
Without energy, our bodies can’t function properly.

Making sure you eat enough food, and the right kind, helps your body to work how it should. High energy foods can also be used to fuel your workouts more efficiently, so that you have the energy needed to push through your workouts.
In this blog, we’ll explore how food is turned into energy, whether there are certain foods that give you energy more quickly, and some of the best food for energy.
HOW IS FOOD TURNED INTO ENERGY?

Everything you eat can be used by your body, but first it needs to be broken down into a usable form. Chewing, along with enzymes in your saliva, helps to break down food into smaller molecules. These are then further broken down by acids and enzymes in the stomach and small intestine. The process for this looks different for different food groups:

Carbohydrates
Carbohydrates are the quickest to break down in the digestive system. They’re broken down into glucose, which is released from the small intestine into the bloodstream. From here, mitochondria in the cells in our bodies can convert glucose into ATP (energy) for fuel. If there is excess glucose, insulin can convert the glucose into glycogen to be stored in the liver and muscles. When blood glucose levels fall, this glycogen can be turned back into glucose and released for energy.

Protein
Protein molecules take longer than carbs to break down, but less time than fat. They’re first broken down into small chains of amino acids in the stomach. As they move through the small intestine, these chains are broken down further into individual amino acids and released into the bloodstream.
While these amino acids can be converted into glucose, the body prefers to use them to repair tissue and build muscle and will only convert to energy if there are more amino acids than the body needs, or a lack of glucose available to use. Excess amino acids can also be converted into fat and stored in the body.

Fat
Unlike protein and carbohydrates, fats cannot be converted into glucose. Instead, they are broken down into fatty acids by the digestive system, which can take up to six hours (much longer than carbs and protein). These fatty acids can be stored in the fat cells or converted directly into ATP if glucose isn’t available in the body.
WHAT FOODS GIVE MORE ENERGY?

Gram for gram, fats provide the most energy at 9 calories, while protein and carbohydrates both provide 4 calories per gram. However, carbohydrates are digested quicker and can be converted into energy quicker than fats and protein and are the body’s preferred energy source.
All foods help contribute towards your energy levels, but when and what you eat can determine how you feel in the short- and long-term.

Eating a chocolate bar will give you energy quickly, but it will likely be followed by a sugar crash, so it’s not a great option if you want energy throughout the day. On the other hand, eating a fat-heavy meal will keep you full for longer, but you might feel sluggish in the short-term.

Pairing complex carbs (carbs that have fibre and other nutrients that help to slow digestion) with protein and fats is the best way to ensure you have consistent energy levels throughout the day. This is because the protein, fibre, and fats help to slow down the release of glucose, ensuring there’s a steady stream of energy available without causing spikes in blood sugar.
Food isn’t the only thing that can boost energy.
ENERGY-BOOSTING FOODS FOR WORKOUTS

Eating balanced meals and snacks throughout the day will help to keep your energy levels consistent from morning to night. If you’re looking for an extra burst of energy to help power your workouts, food can also help with this!

Tailoring your pre-workout meals and snacks is a great way to make sure you have enough energy available to get you through your exercises. We already know from above that carbohydrates are key for readily available energy, but where does protein and fats fit in?
What you eat will depend on how long it is before your workout:

4+ hours
If it’s going to be 4 or more hours before your workout, you want to get a good portion of complex carbs and protein, and a little bit of fat. This will help to ensure you still have glucose available to use for energy but won’t be feeling full. Examples of balanced meals include:
Chicken with sweet potato and veg roasted in oil
Lean mince burgers with homecooked chips and salad
Turkey mince Bolognese with wholewheat pasta
Check out our healthy recipes for more balanced meals and how to make them. Experiment with how long it takes you to digest your meals so you can tailor your portion sizes accordingly.

2-3 hours
The focus here should be mostly on complex carbs, with a little protein. Keep portion sizes modest, as you don’t want to still be digesting or full when exercising.
Beans on toast
Egg on toast
Fruit and Greek yoghurt
Porridge with fruit

1-2 hours
This close to a workout, keep it simple and carbohydrate only. Anything that takes longer to digest will still be in your stomach which can nausea.
Fruit
Toast with honey
Cereal with low fat milk

0-1 hours
Ideally, leave at least 30 minutes between eating and working out as the energy won’t be available otherwise! Simple carbs are the quickest to digest, so stick to things like:
High sugar fruits
Coconut water
Toast with honey

During 
If you are exercising for long periods of time (for example, during longer runs during Marathon Training ), you will benefit from consuming energy during the exercise to top up your glucose levels.
Sports gels
Sport water
Sweets

By Coach : Zaytouni
Although seasoned runners make it seem simple, it takes effort to begin a running regimen.

There's a long way ahead for rookie runners to go before their new activity becomes second nature. It takes perseverance, commitment, and a little bit of strain in the miles between to get through the growing pains of being a professional runner.
While the fact that running is difficult effort, made even more so when it's not done regularly, contributes to some of this problem, a lack of knowledge hinders many first-time runners.

Purchasing new running shoes is simple, but it might be more difficult to comprehend all the factors influencing your running performance and experience. In addition, there is a lot of false information that misleads newcomers and spreads widely, particularly online.

Although there isn't a magic bullet that will make running simple, any beginner runner may steer clear of several typical errors and better guide their own development with the right advice. The following list contains the top five things a novice runner should know.
1. Strength Training Is Critical To Running Injury-Free
Since running is an aerobic activity, most beginning runners are taught that the greatest way to enhance their running fitness is through cardiovascular training.
Running does, however, also subject muscles, tendons, ligaments, and joints to prolonged stress, and if this stress is not appropriately handled, it can result in injury.

One of the finest methods to maintain your injury-free status and develop your structural system is through strength training. If a weight room is available, strength training is a great way to work out. You may strength train without any equipment by performing lunges, wall squats, leg lifts, and hip thrusts on the floor of your living room.
For novices, the hips and core should get the greatest attention.
IT band discomfort, patella tendonitis (runner's knee), piriformis problems, sciatica, and a host of other common running maladies have all been linked to weak hips, according to research.
You may get started by downloading a free running-specific core workout and a hip strengthening programme for runners.
By adding these workouts to your running routine, you may lower your chance of nagging injuries dramatically.
2. Learn To Run With Proper Form

Thousands of steps can be taken on the streets during a single run. Every stride with poor form causes needless tension on some part of the body, which serves as a haven for injuries and persistent discomfort.
Throughout your body, proper form should be used to maximise your mechanics and reduce the risk of injury as well as increase running efficiency.

For optimal hip extension, the upper body should be slanted slightly forward starting at the ankles.
Swinging your arms freely will help you go forward.
To maximise the elastic energy found in the hip flexors and to enable your foot to make contact with the ground squarely beneath your centre of gravity, you should completely extend your hips.
If your leg is immediately underneath you when your foot hits the ground, it doesn't matter which way it strikes—the heel, midfoot, or forefoot.

Increasing your cadence is the simplest approach to make your own running form excellent.
Count the number of times your left foot touches the ground throughout the first thirty seconds of running. Assume yours was forty. To find the total for 60 seconds, double that amount (80); to find the total for both feet, double that amount again (160). That means your cadence (for that specific running pace) is 160 spm.

If your cadence is below 170 spm, try to raise it by five percent. After this starts to seem natural, try increasing your cadence by an additional 5% until you can comfortably walk between 170 and 180 steps per minute.

You might think considering enrolling in our 6-week running form course if you struggle with your form or would like to learn more about running with improved mechanics.
3. Focus On Your Breathing
When running, your mouth should always be the primary method of breathing in and out. This enables you to absorb as much oxygen as possible.
Another useful indicator of how hard you are working in relation to your present level of cardiovascular fitness is how well you are breathing.

For an easy run, a training zone with a 3:3 breathing pattern is suitable. This implies that you will inhale three times and exhale three times each. You're probably going too hard for an easy run day if your breathing is quicker than this.
You may simply evaluate the rhythm of your breathing and make any adjustments if you're not sure how hard you're running.
4. Learn To Pace Yourself
Pacing is crucial to success in both training and races. Regretfully, most runners learn how to pace well by "feel," which can be hard to develop until you've ran a lot.

It might be challenging to determine your pace when there are hundreds or even thousands of runners on the race track. The harm could already be done by the time you get to a mileage marker where you can figure out your pace.
You may train yourself to know what your optimal speed feels like throughout your workouts, however this takes time to perfect. You may measure your pace using your breathing and foot rhythm, and if you have a GPS, you can track it on a regular basis.

Just be careful not to stare at the GPS for too long. You want to learn how to pace yourself naturally, so pay attention to how you're going, check your speed every two or three minutes, and make necessary adjustments until you can pace yourself with ease.
5. Make Wise Mileage Increases
Many runners, and some coaches as well, may use the 10 percent rule as the benchmark for raising weekly distance.

According to this guideline, runners shouldn't increase their weekly distance by more than 10% from the previous week. However, a large body of data indicates that this rule may not be as trustworthy as people would think.

You can't base your decision only on distance because there are a lot more aspects to consider. For example, hard running surfaces put far more pressure on the body than dirt trails do, therefore when increasing mileage on cement routes, considerably greater caution is advised. How much or how little distance you log depends on a number of factors, including your running form, physical fitness, and the cushioning in your shoes. 
You should listen to your body and not push yourself too hard if it hurts in your shins, knees, hips, or other structures. In some situations, you might be able to tolerate an increase of 30 to 40 percent.
A single injury might cause a lot more of a setback than the few extra kilometres you add to a week.

For runners, self-motivation is an excellent weapon, but it must be used with caution and a health-conscious mindset.
If you're just starting out, remember these five things when you approach your first few weeks of jogging. You'll be considerably more likely to finish your workout without getting hurt or giving up.
